To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

urinary albumin excretion (UAE) within the normal range was an independent risk for development of kidney disease within the first 6 months of HIV infection in a prospective study of HIV-infected men.
the use of the albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) in the normal range (0.3–0.7 mg/mg) is associated with an independent increased risk of kidney disease in the near future in HIV-infected individuals.

the use of the 24-hour urine collection method to measure albuminuria is not recommended for HIV-infected patients, and that a single spot urine sample is sufficient to measure albumin excretion in this population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the kidney in the pathogenesis of HIV infection and the role of HIV infection in the pathogenesis and progression of kidney disease.
the development and evaluation of a novel approach for the detection of kidney disease.
the development of a new class of non-linear models for the analysis of longitudinal data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to support or refute the use of antihypertensive medications in the management of hypertension in patients with chronic kidney disease.
the use of a combination of the above-mentioned drugs is the best treatment for the management of hypertension in patients infected with HIV.
albuminuria in the normal range is a risk factor for near-term development and progression of kidney disease in people with HIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

albuminuria is an independent predictor of near-term kidney disease in HIV patients with normal urinary albumin excretion (UAE), and that this association may be mediated through the effect of albuminuria on renal hemodynamic changes and/or the progression of renal fibrosis.
albuminuria is a strong risk factor for kidney disease in HIV infection.
the albuminuria is a risk factor for the progression of kidney disease in the HIV-infected individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of kidney disease progression is not only related to the degree of albuminuria but also to the level of albuminuria within the normal range.
albuminuria is an independent risk factor for the near-term development of chronic kidney disease.
HIV-infected individuals with a normal albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) are still at risk for developing kidney disease, and that the risk is greater in those with a higher ACR.
